title: Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian village as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals
summary:
Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the world’s fastest-warming places

Residents of a remote village in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.

Photograph: Rimante_Hegland/Getty Images/iStockphoto Seascape: the state of our oceans Norway Tap water no longer drinkable in Norwegian village as climate-related thawing releases heavy metals Warning for other Arctic communities as residents told not to use water in Longyearbyen in Svalbard, one of the world’s fastest-warming places Supported by About this content Karen McVeigh Mon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Residents of a remote village in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost. Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard , gets its main drinking water supply from a 1.5 mile-long (2.5km) dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond”. Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond. In the fastest-warming town on the planet you can’t drink the tap water. Here’s why – video Longyearbyen, 800 miles from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate , with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4C a decade. Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost – rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer – and the geology of the former mining settlement. “The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard. View image in fullscreen Marjolaine Verret takes water samples. Photograph: Tonje Emilie Stenstad/The Guardian When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidised and generated acidity, she explained. “The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks.” The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year. The mayor of Longyearbyen, Terje Aunevik, said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic”. Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants. Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched. Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulphate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place. Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous”, government guidelines had to be followed. The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise”, he admitted, with some residents angry at the inconvenience. View image in fullscreen The exposure of bedrock by thawing permafrost has leached metals into the Isdammen lake, the source of Longyearbyen’s water. Photograph: Tonje Emilie Stenstad/The Guardian The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” may be needed. Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around.
